questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Note that plugging in $x=2$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-8}{x-2} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{[{x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-8]^{′}}{[x-2]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{4{x}^{3}-4x}{1} \\  & =4(2)^{3}-4(2) \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}]^{′}}{[{sin}^{2}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x{e}^{-x}-x+2{x}^{2}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[(1-x){e}^{-x}-1+4x]^{′}}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡2x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(x-2){e}^{-x}+4}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{(0-2){e}^{0}+4}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =\frac{-2+4}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}-{9}^{x}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)x}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{4}^{x}-{9}^{x}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)x]}^{′}}{{[1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4-{9}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡9-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4-{9}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡9-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}-{9}^{x}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)x}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4-{9}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡9-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4-{9}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡9-(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9)]}^{′}}{{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)]}^{′}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)^{2}-{9}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡9)^{2}}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)^{2}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡9)^{2}}{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}((\operatorname{ln}⁡4)^{2}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡9)^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}]^{′}}{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}(-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})}{(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =3{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{e}^{3/{x}^{2}}\cancel{(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}}{\cancel{(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}} \\  & =3{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}{e}^{3/{x}^{2}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)]^{′}}{[\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}{2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)})(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)})}{2(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x){(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))}^{2}}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\cdot 4{sin}^{2}⁡(x){cos}^{2}⁡(x)}{2{sin}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{4{cos}^{3}⁡(x)\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)}}{2\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}2{cos}^{3}⁡(x) \\  & =2{cos}^{3}⁡(0) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac {\left[\sin^2 (2x)\right]'}{[x^2]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{2\cdot \sin (2x) \cdot\cos (2x)\cdot 2}{2x}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}{2\cos (2x)} \cdot \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\cos(2\cdot 0)\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}
}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ But that's okay, because we can just apply L'Hopital's rule again! We get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&=  2\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac {[\sin (2x)]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&=  2\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac {2\cos (2x)}{1}\[5pt]
&= 4\cos(2\cdot 0)\
&=4.
}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are
$\displaystyle
 \lim_{x\to 0}  \ln\left(x^2\right) = -\infty$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{2}{x^2} = \infty$ respectively,
so we have the case $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{\left(1/x^2\right)\cdot 2x}{-\left({4}/{x^3}\right)}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{x^{-2} \cdot 2x}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{2x^{-1}}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}  \lim_{x\to 0} {x^2}\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\[5pt]
&= 0.
}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\dfrac{\infty}{\infty},$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {x^6}{5x^6-4} &= \lim_{x\to\infty}  \dfrac {[x^6]'}{[5x^6-4]'}\
&= \lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {6x^5}{5(6x^5)-0}\
&=  \lim_{x\to \infty}  \dfrac {1}{5}\
&= \dfrac{1}{5}.
}
$$
